claims.text: Atomic-scale chemical fluctuations induce local lattice distortions in high-entropy alloys.
Local lattice distortions govern superconducting behavior in high-entropy alloys.
The initial material is a high-entropy alloy containing equal atomic proportions of at least five principal elements.
Systematic composition variation can introduce controlled levels of atomic-scale chemical fluctuations.
The comparison is conducted at cryogenic temperatures below the alloy's superconducting critical temperature.
The relevant structural mediator is local lattice distortion around solute atoms.
Local lattice distortions modify the electronic density of states.
Changes in the electronic density of states influence the superconducting pairing mechanism.
Alloys with greater atomic-scale chemical fluctuations will have higher superconducting critical temperatures.
Alloys with greater atomic-scale chemical fluctuations will have higher critical current densities.
The baseline is a high-entropy alloy composition selected to have minimal atomic-scale chemical fluctuations.
The hypothesis applies to high-entropy alloys having FCC or BCC crystal structures.
The hypothesis may not generalize to alloys with other crystal structures or significant phase separation.
The relationship between local lattice distortion and superconducting behavior is not well understood.
The hypothesis is falsified if multiple alloy compositions show no correlation between atomic-scale chemical fluctuations and superconducting properties.
